Original instructions

First setup About this manual

Source Robotics d.o.o. publishes this document for the MSG compliant AI stepper gripper. It is revised as the gripper and its firmware change; the document number, the gripper release, the firmware, the revision and the date above identify the version you are reading, and the document history on the About page says what changed. The version selector in the header switches between gripper releases. The gripper runs the STEPFOC driver's firmware: take care that the firmware named under Applies to matches what the gripper reports. The text and the images are licensed CC BY-SA 4.0, the code examples MIT.

The MSG is open source, and that is important to us. Everything the gripper is made of is published: the CAD and print files, the bill of materials, the assembly instructions, the driver's firmware and the software that drives it. Buy the gripper assembled, or build one yourself; change the jaws or the body for your application and fit it to any robot. Build your own is the order to do it in.

    Motor GUI in the browser, then calibrate, activate, move: from the box to a gripper that opens and closes on command.

  • The manual

    Safety, Technical data, Installation, First setup, Operation, Maintenance, Firmware, Troubleshooting.

  • On a robot

    PAROL6 and PAR6, ROS 2, Python: the gripper from the robot's own software, from a ROS 2 node, or from your program over CAN.

  • API reference

    The gripper's CAN messages and UART commands, the status bits and the Python library, read from the firmware.

  • Open source: build your own

    Everything is published: print the parts, source the rest from the BOM, assemble, configure the driver. The same manual applies.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text: The MSG gripper is a force-controlled gripper for collaborative and research robots, not a certified safety component. Whoever puts it on a machine is responsible for the risk assessment of the gripper, the robot and everything around them. Read this chapter before you power the gripper; the rules here are the ones that injure a hand or destroy the gripper when they are ignored.

docs.title: Mechanical
docs.text:
The jaws

The jaws are a pinch point. With the current limit at the stepper's rating they close with tens of newtons, enough to crush a finger, and at full speed they travel the whole stroke in well under a second. Never put a finger between the jaws of a powered gripper. Keep hands away during calibration, which moves the jaws over the whole stroke without any command from you.

Start low

Test every new setup with a low current and speed: current 300 to 500 mA, speed 30. Raise them step by step once the application behaves, and never above the stepper's rated current (Force and speed).

Objects

A gripped object that slips, or that the jaws crush, can fly or fall. The grip force is a current limit, not a measurement: a hard object takes the full force, a soft one deforms until the force is reached.

docs.title: Electrical
docs.text:
The cable

The gripper's M8 connector carries 24 V next to the CAN bus. A cable with the wrong pinout, including the cable of the other Source Robotics robot, puts 24 V on the CAN pins and destroys the driver. Use the cable made for your robot or check every pin of your own; see The cable.

Supply

24 V DC. The driver inside tolerates 12 to 29 V, but the gripper's force and speed figures assume 24 V.

Do not unplug a powered gripper

Connect and disconnect the cable with the supply off. Hot-plugging the connector can damage the driver.

docs.title: Temperature
docs.text: The motor has a thermistor in its windings. At 75 °C the driver raises a temperature error and the gripper goes idle; it clears when the motor has cooled and the error is cleared. A gripper holding an object at a high current for long heats up: for a long hold, use the lowest current that holds the object. A self-built gripper without a thermistor in the windings has no protection and can burn out its motor; see Driver configuration.

docs.title: Stopping the gripper
docs.text:
• The E-stop bit of the move command (Send_gripper_data_pack) stops the gripper and raises the gripper E-stop error, which stays until it is cleared.
  • Send_ESTOP to the driver, or #Idle over UART, stops it as well.
  • The CAN watchdog (Send_Watchdog) stops the gripper by itself when the host stops talking, which is the right protection for a program that may crash mid-grip.
  • Cutting the supply releases the grip: a stepper without current holds nothing beyond its own friction, so an object can drop.

None of these is a certified safety function. A machine that can hurt someone needs an emergency stop that cuts the power, independent of the gripper and the robot software.

docs.title: Care
docs.text: The gripper is not waterproof or dustproof: the rail and the racks are open to dust, chips and liquids. Keep it out of wet or dusty places. What to check, and when to grease the mechanism, is in Maintenance.

docs.title: Liability
docs.text: The MSG gripper is sold as a component for people who build their own machines, and its designs are published for people who build the gripper itself. The hardware designs, the firmware and this documentation are provided as they are, without a warranty, and are under development; they may contain errors. Whoever builds or operates a machine with the gripper is responsible for its safe design, assembly and operation. The full disclaimer is in the product repository.

docs.title: Maintenance
docs.text: The gripper needs little: every wearing part is printed, so a worn part is replaced by printing a new one, and the mechanism is a rail, two racks and a pinion that want a little grease now and then. Power the gripper off before any work on it.

docs.title: Before each session
docs.text:
• The jaws sit tight on their carriers, nothing is cracked, the pads or the sponge tape are whole.
  • The cable's M8 nut is tight, the cable has slack for the wrist's full motion and runs clear of the jaws.
  • Nothing lies in the jaws' travel, and the gripper calibration finds both end stops.

docs.title: When the motion gets rough, and every few months of regular use
docs.text:
• Grease. A little lithium grease on the rail and on the rack and pinion. Remove the four screws that hold the linear rail to reach the mechanism, wipe off the old grease and the dust, grease, refit, and move the jaws over the whole stroke by hand before you power up. A grinding noise, a stiff motion or a calibration that stops short of an end are the signs that it is due.
  • Clean with a dry cloth. The gripper is not waterproof or dustproof: keep it out of wet and dusty places, and blow chips out of the rail rather than wash them out.
  • Screws: the jaw screws, the rail screws and the clamp screws of the shaft coupler; threadlocker where the assembly instructions use it.
  • The camera lens, with a lens cloth.

docs.title: Replacing worn parts
docs.text:
The jaws, the pads and every other printed part are in the product repository, Print files; the rail, the carriages, the pinion and the screws are in the BOM. A replacement jaw is the same part as a new one, and the gripper calibration at the next power-up takes care of the end stops.

A stepper or a driver is not serviced but replaced: the stepper by one of the three in the BOM, after which the motor calibration of Driver configuration is run again; the driver by a new STEPFOC driver, configured the same way.

docs.title: Firmware
docs.text: The gripper has no firmware of its own: it runs the STEPFOC driver's firmware with gripper mode turned on. This site describes the firmware release named in the version box on the landing page, for the gripper release the site is versioned by; a new firmware release for the same gripper updates these pages in place.

docs.title: Which release does my gripper run?
docs.text: Over CAN, Send_Respond_Device_Info returns the firmware version as its third byte; over UART, #Info prints Software version: <number>. The compatibility table says which releases go with which Python library and bootloader.

docs.title: Updating
docs.text:
A gripper shipped with firmware 104 or newer carries the driver's bootloader and updates over its CAN cable: the host tells the driver to reset, the bootloader waits two seconds for a host, and the host streams the new image into it. Nothing is opened. The image is stepfoc-firmware-V<number>.bin from the driver's GitHub releases, with a manifest firmware.json and the release notes.

From How a PC with the CANvas adapter Motor GUI over CAN: choose the release, the GUI fetches the image and flashes it a PC, scripted host_tools/bl_flash.py from the bootloader repository, over CAN (slcan or gs_usb adapters) or over the driver's UART port a PAR6 control box the box updates every device on its bus, the gripper included, from its dashboard or tools/flash_motor_firmware.py

The procedure, the bootloader's protocol and what to do when a flash is interrupted are in the STEPFOC documentation: Updating through the bootloader and The bootloader.

Before you update

  • Open the gripper or take the object out: it loses its grip during the update and until it is calibrated and commanded again.
  • An update may clear the driver's configuration (the release notes say so when it does). A bought gripper's configuration is in Driver configuration, so it can be restored; note what #Info prints before you start.
  • Give the gripper a node ID from 0 to 13: the bootloader cannot address 14 or 15.

A gripper whose driver runs firmware 103 or older has no bootloader; it is updated once with a programming adapter on the driver's JTAG pads, inside the housing, as described in Installing the bootloader on an older board. From then on it updates over CAN like any other.

docs.text: The release notes of every STEPFOC release up to the one this site describes are in the appendix, Firmware release notes.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: By symptom. The error flags and what clears them are in Errors and recovery.

docs.title: The gripper does not answer
docs.text: Symptom Check nothing at all the 24 V on the cable; the cable's pinout (a wrong one has destroyed the driver already); the node ID the host uses; 1 Mbit/s on the adapter; the termination (about 60 Ω across CANH and CANL, unpowered) answers, then stops answering the watchdog ran out and the host did not notice; a loose M8 connector; a second device with the same node ID the GUI shows No connection the COM port of the CANvas adapter; another program holding the port; the CAN ID in the GUI

docs.title: It does not move
docs.text: Symptom Check calibrated, activated, no error, no motion the action bit of the command is 0; the command is identical to the previous one (change the speed or the current by one to repeat a move) Not calibrated after power-up normal: run the gripper calibration an error is shown Errors and recovery: clear it, then look at the cause if it comes back the driver reports Not calibrated in State_of_Errors and #Error the stepper itself is not calibrated (a self-built gripper): Driver configuration

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text: Symptom Cause the jaws move to one end and stop; after 24 s the gripper is still not calibrated the other end is blocked, or the mechanism is too stiff for the calibration's 500 mA: a tight rail, a pinion pressed too hard into the racks, debris in the racks the jaws jitter and do not travel a phase of the stepper not connected (self-built), or the stepper not calibrated 255 is not fully closed, or 0 not fully open something stopped the jaws short of the end during calibration; calibrate again with the stroke free

docs.title: The grip
docs.text: Symptom Cause the object slips the current too low for the object; the jaw faces: sponge tape or the TPU pad the object is crushed the current too high; a hard object takes the full force at once object detected while nothing is there the current limit too low for the mechanism's friction at that speed; raise the current a little or lower the speed the gripper stops with a temperature error after a while a long hold at a high current; hold with the lowest current that keeps the object the jaws creep or hum when holding the position loop against a hard object; lower the current, or hold a soft object with a position slightly beyond the contact

docs.title: Noise and heat
docs.text: A stepper under field-oriented control is quiet; a grinding noise is the rack and pinion without grease, or debris. The motor gets warm in use and hot under a long grip; the thermistor stops it at 75 °C. A self-built gripper without a thermistor in the windings has no such protection.

docs.title: After a firmware update
docs.text: If the gripper does not calibrate or behaves oddly after an update, check the driver's configuration with #Info over UART: gripper mode (#Gripper 1), the thermistor (#Term 1), the motor calibration. A release note says when an update clears the configuration; Driver configuration restores it.

docs.title: Getting help
docs.text: Support says where to ask and what to include; the gripper's status and #Info's output are the first things.

docs.title: About this manual
docs.text:
The MSG Gripper Manual covers the MSG compliant AI stepper gripper from unpacking to a gripper that works on a robot: mounting and cabling, the first setup with Motor GUI, control over CAN and UART, from Python, from ROS 2 and from the PAROL6 and PAR6 robots, and firmware updates. It is written for a maker, a student or an engineer who can plug in a cable and run a Python script. Read Safety before you power anything; First setup is the shortest path to a gripper that moves.

The gripper is a STEPFOC stepper driver in gripper mode. The driver itself, from its full command set to its calibration and its bootloader, is documented on the STEPFOC site; this manual links there instead of repeating it.

docs.title: Finding your way
docs.text:
Four tabs: MSG Gripper Manual, the numbered chapters, read from the start; API reference, the gripper's CAN messages, UART commands, status bits and Python calls, for looking things up (the driver's complete reference is on the STEPFOC site); Guides, worked examples; Support, help and problem reports.

The dropdown next to the site name switches between gripper releases, and a page of an older release says so in a bar at the top. The repository card in the header opens the product repository; every page ends with a link to edit it and one to report a problem with it.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Action bit A bit of the move command: 1 carries out the move, 0 leaves the gripper idle with the command stored. Activated A flag the gripper keeps, set by the activate bit of the move command or by #Gripact. A move is carried out only while the gripper is activated and calibrated. CAN ID (node ID) The address of the gripper on the CAN bus, 0 to 13; every gripper ships as 0. It occupies bits 10 to 7 of the 11-bit CAN frame identifier; the command ID occupies bits 6 to 1 and the error bit is bit 0. CANvas Source Robotics' USB-to-CAN adapter. It appears as a serial port and speaks slcan, which python-can, Motor GUI and the ROS 2 driver use. Current limit (grip force) The current, in mA, the driver may put into the motor during a move. Torque is current times the motor's torque constant, so the current limit sets the force with which the jaws press on an object. Driver The STEPFOC board on the back of the gripper's stepper: field-oriented control of the motor, the gripper state machine and the CAN and UART interfaces. The gripper's firmware is the driver's firmware. E-stop bit A bit of the move command. 1 stops the gripper and raises the gripper E-stop error, which stays until it is cleared and a command with the bit at 0 arrives. Error bit Bit 0 of every CAN frame identifier the driver sends: 1 while any error is active. Field-oriented control (FOC) Controlling the stepper's current as a vector relative to the rotor, from the driver's encoder. It turns the stepper into a motor whose torque is known and limited, which is what makes a force-controlled gripper out of it. Firmware release One build of the STEPFOC firmware, numbered 103, 104, 105, … and tagged V103, V104, … in the driver's repository. #Info prints the release a gripper runs. This documentation describes one release; the version selector switches between them. Gripper calibration The routine (Send_gripper_calibrate, #Gripcal) that opens the jaws fully, then closes them fully, at low force, and records both end stops as positions 0 and 255. Needed after every power-up. Gripper mode The driver's mode in which it runs a gripper (#Gripper 1, saved): move commands with a jaw position, a speed and a current limit, and object detection. Motor calibration The driver's own calibration of the stepper (#Cal): the pole pairs, resistance and inductance entered, the encoder aligned, the motor constants measured. Done once, at the factory or when you build the gripper; not to be confused with the gripper calibration. Object detection The gripper's report of why the jaws stopped: 0 still moving, 1 an object stopped them while closing, 2 an object stopped them while opening, 3 they reached the commanded position. Position The jaw position as the gripper commands and reports it: 0 fully open, 255 fully closed, linear in between. Rack and pinion The gripper's mechanism: a pinion on the motor shaft meshes with two racks that run on the linear rail in opposite directions, so one motor moves both jaws symmetrically. Speed The speed of a move, 0 to 255, mapped by the firmware to 500 to 60000 encoder ticks per second of the motor. Stroke How far each jaw carrier travels from fully open to fully closed: 55, 105 or 155 mm, set by the rail length. Timeout error (watchdog) The driver's CAN watchdog, as the gripper reports it: when the watchdog is set (Send_Watchdog) and no valid frame arrives in time, the gripper stops and raises it. Watchdog A timer the driver resets with every valid CAN frame it receives. When it is set and runs out, the gripper reports a timeout error and stops.

docs.title: Build your own
docs.text:
The MSG is open source, and that is important to us. Everything the gripper is made of is published in the product repository under the CERN Open Hardware Licence: the STEP files of every part, the print files, the bill of materials with a link for every item, the assembly video, and the URDF and MJCF models. The driver's firmware and the software that drives the gripper are open source too. A gripper you build is the same gripper as the one from the shop, and this manual applies to it; change the jaws, the camera mount or the body for your application, or fit the gripper to a robot it was not designed for. This page is the order to do it in.

Warning

A self-built gripper is yours to make safe: the thermistor in the windings, the current within the stepper's maximum, and the Safety chapter apply to it as to a bought one. The gripper is in beta: expect rough edges in the hardware and the software.

docs.title: 2. Print the parts
docs.text:
Variant Folders in STEP files every gripper Common parts: the coupler plate and ring cover (or ring_cover-PAROL6), the camera mount and lid, the jaw blocker, the stepper spacer, the connector lid your rail Linear rail dependant parts/<rail>: the body and the two jaw carriers your stepper Stepper dependant parts/<stepper>: the stepper cover, and the spacer for the 21.5 mm stepper the jaws Gripper jaws attachment: one of the designs, mirrored for the other side (Jaws)

The Print files folder has the same parts as 3MF, ready to slice. PETG, 25 % infill for everything; TPU for the jaw pads.

docs.title: 3. Source the rest
docs.text: The BOM lists every part with a link: the stepper of your variant, the STEPFOC driver, the encoder magnet, the thermistor and the thermal cement, the MGN7 rail and two carriages, the pinion (32 DP, 21 teeth, 5 mm bore), the shaft coupler, the M8 connector and the short XH and ZH cables that connect the driver inside, the brass inserts and the screws, the camera, and the sponge tape for the jaws. The screws for the stepper depend on its length (22, 40 or 60 mm M3).

docs.title: 4. Configure the driver
docs.text: Before the pinion goes in: mount the driver on the stepper with its magnet, calibrate the motor, set up gripper mode and the thermistor, and save. Driver configuration is the procedure; the magnet and the driver's mounting are in the STEPFOC documentation. Place the thermistor bead in the windings with thermal cement and route its leads to the driver's thermistor connector.

docs.title: 5. Assemble
docs.text: Follow the assembly video. The rail with its two carriages goes into the body, the racks onto the carriages, the stepper with the pinion into the body so that the pinion meshes with both racks, the driver's power and CAN cables to the M8 connector in its lid, the stepper cover over the driver with the termination switch reachable through its opening, the coupler plate with the shaft coupler on the back, and the jaws on the carriers.

docs.title: 6. Cable, calibrate, move
docs.text: An M8 4-pin cable to your robot or your supply and CAN adapter: The cable has the wiring diagrams and the warning about the two robots' cables. Power up, calibrate the gripper, activate it and move it at a low current, as in Calibrate, activate, move. If the calibration does not find both end stops, the mechanism is too stiff: loosen the rail, check the pinion's depth in the racks, grease.

docs.title: The gripper at a glance
docs.text:
The MSG is a two-jaw parallel gripper driven by a NEMA 17 stepper under field-oriented control. The STEPFOC driver on the back of the stepper regulates the motor's current, so a move sets not only where the jaws go and how fast, but how hard they press: the current limit is the grip force. The jaws stop on an object, hold it with that force, and the driver reports that an object was found. A camera mount looks between the jaws, for teleoperation and for training vision-language-action models.

Figure 1: The MSG gripper with the 150 mm rail and the camera mount.

docs.title: The parts
docs.text:
Part What it does NEMA 17 stepper motor, 21.5, 40 or 60 mm long the actuator; its length sets the grip force: about 31, 50 or 76 N at its maximum current STEPFOC driver on the back of the stepper field-oriented control of the stepper, the gripper state machine, the CAN and UART interfaces Pinion on the motor shaft, two racks on a linear rail the pinion turns, the two racks move in opposite directions: the jaws open and close symmetrically MGN7 linear rail, 100, 150 or 200 mm carries the jaws; its length sets the stroke Jaws printed, in several shapes, with a soft TPU pad or solid; yours to adapt Thermistor in the motor windings temperature protection: the gripper stops at 75 °C M8 4-pin connector 24 V and the CAN bus, one cable to the robot Camera mount an OV9732 USB camera module looking between the jaws Coupler plate mounts the gripper on an 8 mm shaft, or on the PAROL6 wrist with its own cover

The driver's status LED and its UART port are inside the housing; the CAN termination switch is reachable through the stepper cover (CAN termination).

docs.title: What the firmware does
docs.text: After power-up the gripper calibrates by finding both end stops. Then it takes move commands: a position from 0 (open) to 255 (closed), a speed from 0 to 255 and a current limit in mA. When the jaws stop short of the target with the current at its limit, an object is in the way and is held; when they reach the target, the position is held. Every answer carries the state: moving, object found while closing or opening, or at the position. The gripper stops itself on an over-temperature, an E-stop bit from the host, a CAN watchdog that runs out, and every fault the driver detects. How the gripper works and Errors and recovery have the details.

docs.title: How it is controlled
docs.text:
• CAN, 1 Mbit/s, on the same cable as the power: one message moves the gripper and is answered with its state. From a PC with the CANvas adapter, from a ROS 2 node, from PAROL6 or PAR6, or from your own controller. See Over CAN.
  • Python, the Spectral-BLDC library on top of CAN. See With Python.
  • Motor GUI in the browser: connect, calibrate, open and close, watch the plots. See Motor GUI.
  • UART, the driver's serial port inside the housing: for configuration, and for a self-built gripper. See Over UART.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text:
The gripper is modular in two ways: the length of the linear rail sets the stroke, the length of the stepper sets the force. Any rail goes with any stepper, and the body comes in black or grey; the body, the jaw carriers and the stepper cover are printed for the chosen combination.

Figure 2: The three rail lengths and the stroke each gives. BlackGrey

Figure 3: The nine combinations of rail and stepper, black body: 55, 105 and 155 mm of stroke across, the 21.5, 40 and 60 mm steppers down.

The same nine combinations, grey body.

docs.title: Rail length and stroke
docs.text:
Rail Stroke Printed parts 100 mm 55 mm MSG_Gripper_body_100mm, gripper_jaw_100mm_L/R 150 mm 105 mm MSG_Gripper_body_150mm, gripper_jaw_150mm_L/R 200 mm 155 mm MSG_Gripper_body_200mm, gripper_jaw_200mm_L/R

The stroke is the distance between the jaw carriers from fully open to fully closed; the opening between the jaw faces depends on the jaws you fit (Jaws). A longer rail makes the gripper wider and a little heavier and does not change the force.

docs.title: Stepper length and force
docs.text:
Stepper Motor Maximum current Torque constant Grip force at the maximum current Printed parts 21.5 mm 17HS08-1004S 1.5 A 0.17 Nm/A about 31 N Stepper_cover_21_5mm, Stepper_spacer_21_5 40 mm 17HS16-2004S1 2.0 A 0.21 Nm/A about 50 N Stepper_cover_40mm 60 mm 17HS24-2104S 2.1 A 0.30 Nm/A about 76 N Stepper_cover_60mm

A longer stepper gives more torque and so more grip force, at the price of weight and length behind the gripper. The force is proportional to the current limit you command, with the slope of the stepper's torque constant; the curves and the formula are in Force and speed. The current limit must stay within the stepper's maximum.

docs.title: Grasps
docs.text: The gripper grips from the outside (the jaws close on the object) and from the inside (the jaws open inside a hollow object). Both are the same move command with a different target; object detection reports while closing for the first and while opening for the second.

docs.title: The camera
docs.text:
The camera mount on top of the body carries an OV9732 USB camera module (100° version in the BOM), looking down between the jaws. It is a plain USB camera with its own cable, independent of the gripper's electronics; the mount and its lid are printed parts (camera extension, camera_lid), and a gripper without a camera simply leaves them off.

Figure 4: The gripper on a PAROL6 and what its camera sees.

docs.title: The gripper
docs.text:
The MSG gripper is sold assembled, calibrated and configured in the Source Robotics shop, in the rail and stepper combination you choose, in black or grey. It ships with the current STEPFOC firmware and the bootloader installed, its driver in gripper mode and its stepper calibrated; the gripper calibration (finding the end stops) runs after every power-up and is part of normal use.

Or build it. The MSG is open source, and that is important to us: the CAD and print files, the bill of materials, the assembly video, the firmware and the software are all published. Build your own is the order to do it in.

docs.title: What is in the box
docs.text: The gripper, assembled, calibrated and configured, in the rail, stepper and colour you ordered, with the camera module when ordered. Not in the box: the jaws, which you print from the repository or buy in the shop; the cable, sold separately; a CAN adapter for a PC.

docs.title: A cable and a 24 V supply
docs.text:
The gripper is powered and controlled through one M8 4-pin cable: 24 V, GND, CANH, CANL.

Where the gripper goes Cable PAROL6 the PAROL6 gripper cable from the shop PAR6 the PAR6 gripper cable (the shop; coming soon), wired differently from the PAROL6 one a bench, or your own robot a cable you make from an M8 4-pin connector and four wires, see The cable

The two robot cables differ

PAROL6 and PAR6 put the four signals on different pins. A cable for the wrong robot, or a self-made cable with a wrong pin, puts 24 V where the CAN bus belongs and destroys the gripper's driver. Check the pinout before you plug in a cable for the first time.

On the bench, a 24 V supply with a current limit (2 A is plenty for one gripper) is the safest source.

docs.title: A CAN interface
docs.text: The gripper talks CAN. On a robot, the robot's control board provides the bus. On a PC, the CANvas USB-to-CAN adapter does; it shows up as a serial port and works with Motor GUI, the Python library and the ROS 2 driver. Any adapter that python-can supports works with the library.

docs.title: Software
docs.text:
• Motor GUI, motorgui.com, in the browser over the CANvas adapter: the recommended tool to test and set up a gripper, with a gripper panel for the MSG and the SSG-48; see Motor GUI. The earlier SSG-gripper-GUI, a Python program, is legacy.
  • Python: pip install Spectral-BLDC, the library the ROS 2 driver is built on; see With Python.
  • ROS 2: the msg_gripper_ros2 package; see With ROS 2.
  • PAROL6 and PAR6: the robots' own software drives the gripper; see On PAROL6 and PAR6.
  • For a self-built gripper: a 3.3 V USB-to-serial adapter (serial adapter) for the driver's UART port, to configure the driver with Motor GUI or a terminal; see Driver configuration.

docs.title: Optional
docs.text:
• Jaws for your objects: the printed jaws in the repository (solid, hollow, or with a TPU pad), sponge tape for the gripping faces, or your own design; see Jaws.
  • A camera: an OV9732 USB module for the camera mount; see Variants.

docs.title: Technical data
docs.text: The numbers: the specifications of the gripper and its variants, what the current and speed settings mean in newtons and millimetres per second, the connector and its pinout, and where the CAD files are.

docs.title: Connector and pinout
docs.text:
The gripper has one connector, an M8 4-pin male on the side of the body, and one cable: 24 V and the CAN bus.

Figure 7: The M8 connector on the gripper body and its four signals: 24V, GND, CANH, CANL. Signal What it is 24V the supply, 24 V DC GND the supply's return and the CAN bus reference CANH, CANL the CAN bus, 1 Mbit/s

Which pin of the M8 carries which signal is shown in Figure 7. The cables for PAROL6 and PAR6 are wired differently at the robot end; The cable has the wiring diagram of each.

The wrong cable destroys the driver

A cable with 24 V on a CAN pin destroys the driver inside the gripper the moment it is powered. Use the cable made for your robot; check a self-made cable pin by pin against Figure 7 and the wiring diagram before you plug it in.

docs.title: Inside the housing
docs.text: The STEPFOC driver's own connectors are inside: its UART port (3.3 V, JST SH, 4 pins) under the coupler plate, used to configure a self-built gripper (Over UART), and its CAN termination switch, reachable through an opening in the stepper cover (CAN termination). The driver's pinout is in the STEPFOC documentation.

docs.title: Dimensions and CAD
docs.text:
The gripper's dimensions depend on the rail and the stepper: the rail length sets the width (100, 150 or 200 mm plus the jaws at full opening), the stepper length what sticks out behind the body. The STEP files of every part and of the whole gripper in each variant are in the product repository, and are the reference for anything that has to fit:

  • STEP files: Common parts (the coupler plate, the ring covers, the camera mount, the jaw blocker, the stepper spacer), Linear rail dependant parts (the body and the jaw carriers per rail length), Stepper dependant parts (the covers and spacers per stepper length), Gripper jaws attachment (the jaw designs), Tools (the magnet tool).
  • Print files: the same parts as 3MF, ready to slice.
Figure 8: The STEP model of the gripper, seen from the coupler plate.

docs.title: For simulation
docs.text:
The MSG_gripper_description folder has a URDF of the gripper for ROS 2 and Gazebo and an MJCF for MuJoCo 3.1.3 and newer, with a scene file.

CAD and downloads lists everything that can be downloaded.

docs.title: Force and speed
docs.text: A move command carries a current limit in mA and a speed from 0 to 255. This page says what they mean in newtons and millimetres per second.

docs.title: Grip force
docs.text:
The driver limits the motor's current to the value you command, so the torque the motor produces is limited to \(T = K_t \, I_q\), with \(K_t\) the motor's torque constant in Nm/A (#Kt prints what the driver uses) and \(I_q\) the current limit in amperes (the command is in mA). The pinion turns the torque into the force the jaws press with:

\[ F = \frac{K_t \, I_q}{r}, \qquad r = 8.3\ \text{mm} \]

\(r\) is the pitch radius of the pinion (32 DP, 21 teeth). The force is proportional to the current, with a slope set by the stepper:

Stepper Motor \(K_t\) Force per ampere Maximum current Grip force at the maximum current 21.5 mm 17HS08-1004S 0.17 Nm/A 20 N/A 1.5 A about 31 N 40 mm 17HS16-2004S1 0.21 Nm/A 25 N/A 2.0 A about 50 N 60 mm 17HS24-2104S 0.30 Nm/A 36 N/A 2.1 A about 76 N Figure 6: The grip force against the current limit for the three steppers, each up to its maximum current, from the formula above.

The curves are computed from the torque constants, not measured with a force gauge: a measurement on your gripper is the only exact calibration, and a self-built gripper with another stepper has another \(K_t\). Below about 150 mA the motor does not move reliably, so the usable range starts at a few newtons. Motor GUI commands up to 1500 mA; the full force of the 40 mm and 60 mm steppers needs a command from Python or over CAN.

The force is a limit, not a controlled value: a hard object takes the full force the moment the jaws touch it; a soft object is squeezed until the force is reached.

Stay within the stepper's maximum

The firmware does not clamp the gripper's current. A current above the stepper's maximum overheats the motor; the thermistor stops the gripper at 75 °C, but a motor driven far over its rating heats faster than the thermistor follows. The maximums are in the table above.

docs.title: Payload
docs.text:
The grip force is not the weight the gripper can lift. An object held by friction between the two jaws is held by \(2\,\mu F\), with \(\mu\) the friction coefficient between the jaw faces and the object, and a safety factor \(S\) covers what the robot adds:

\[ W = \frac{2\,\mu\,F}{S} \]

With a conservative \(\mu\) = 0.3 (a hard printed jaw on steel or smooth plastic; a TPU pad or sponge tape on a dry object gives more) and \(S\) = 2, the 60 mm stepper at 76 N holds about 23 N, 2.3 kg, and the 21.5 mm stepper at 31 N about 9 N, 0.9 kg. That is the weight held at rest: a robot accelerating at 1 g doubles the load, and an emergency stop decelerates harder than any programmed move. The friction coefficient is the big unknown; measure it with your jaws on your object, or close on the object's shape (a form-fit grip) and let friction be the reserve.

docs.title: Speed
docs.text:
The speed byte of a move is mapped by the firmware to the motor's speed in encoder ticks per second, linearly from 500 at speed 0 to 60000 at speed 255:

\[ \text{ticks/s} = 500 + \frac{60000 - 500}{255}\, C \]

The motor's encoder has 16384 ticks per revolution, so the angular speed is \(\omega = \text{ticks/s} / 16384 \times 2\pi\) and each jaw moves at

\[ v = \omega \, r \] Speed byte Motor speed Each jaw moves at The jaws close at 0 500 ticks/s, 0.03 rev/s 1.6 mm/s 3 mm/s 30 7500 ticks/s, 0.46 rev/s 24 mm/s 48 mm/s 128 30400 ticks/s, 1.9 rev/s 97 mm/s 190 mm/s 255 60000 ticks/s, 3.7 rev/s 190 mm/s 380 mm/s

Both jaws move, so the gap closes at twice the speed of one jaw. At speed 255 a 105 mm stroke takes about half a second. The gripper calibration runs at speed 40 and 500 mA.

docs.title: Position
docs.text: The position byte is linear over the stroke: 0 is the fully open end stop found by the gripper calibration, 255 the fully closed one. One step of the byte is the stroke divided by 255: 0.22 mm on the 100 mm rail, 0.41 mm on the 150 mm rail, 0.61 mm on the 200 mm rail. The driver considers the position reached within 5 encoder ticks, about 0.03 mm.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Putting the gripper on a robot: the mounting, the cable that carries its power and its CAN bus, the jaws for your objects, and the CAN termination.

docs.title: In this chapter
docs.text:
• Mounting on a robot
  • The cable
  • Jaws
  • CAN termination

When all of it is done, continue with First setup.

docs.title: The cable
docs.text:
One cable with an M8 4-pin connector powers the gripper and carries its CAN bus. The robot end differs from robot to robot.

PAROL6 and PAR6 cables are different

The two robots put the four signals on different pins of their gripper port. The PAROL6 cable in a PAR6, or the other way round, puts 24 V on the CAN bus and destroys the gripper's driver. Use the cable sold for your robot, and check a self-made cable pin by pin.

docs.title: The cables from the shop
docs.text: Robot Cable PAROL6 PAROL6 gripper cable PAR6 the PAR6 gripper cable, coming to the shop

docs.title: Making your own
docs.text:
For a bench setup, another robot, or a replacement, the cable is four wires between an M8 4-pin female connector at the gripper and whatever the other end needs:

Part Quantity BOM 26 AWG 4-wire twisted-pair cable, 0.15 mm², shielded about 0.4 m cable M8 4-pin female cable connector (the gripper has the male) 1 connector M8 4-pin male cable connector, for a robot with an M8 port 1 the same listing

Wire it as the diagram for your robot shows. Pin 1 to 4 are the numbers moulded into the M8 connectors; the colours are those of the cable in the BOM.

PAROL6PAR6Bench or your own robot

Figure 11: The PAROL6 cable: the pins are crossed between the two ends.

Figure 12: The PAR6 cable: pin to pin.

Connect the gripper's 24V and GND to a 24 V supply and its CANH and CANL to your CAN interface; on a PC that is the CANvas adapter's CAN terminals. Connector and pinout shows which pin of the gripper's connector is which signal. Twist the CAN pair, keep the cable short at 1 Mbit/s, and terminate the bus at both ends (CAN termination).

Connect the shield at one end only. Check continuity and the absence of shorts between all four pins before the first power-up.

docs.title: Handling
docs.text: Plug and unplug with the supply off. Route the cable along the robot with enough slack for the wrist's full motion, and keep it away from the jaws' travel.

docs.title: CAN termination
docs.text:
A CAN bus needs a 120 Ω resistor at each of its two ends. The gripper's driver has one, on a switch that is reachable through an opening in the stepper cover: ON connects the resistor, 1 disconnects it.

Figure 15: The termination switch of the driver, seen through the stepper cover. The gripper is Switch the last node on a robot's bus, at the end of the arm ON alone on a bench bus with the CANvas adapter (which has its own termination) ON in the middle of a bus, with other nodes after it 1 (off)

A bus with the right termination measures about 60 Ω between CANH and CANL with everything unpowered. A missing or doubled termination shows up as lost frames and a gripper that answers only sometimes.

docs.title: Jaws
docs.text:
The jaws bolt to the two carriers on the rail and are yours to adapt. The product repository has three designs, all in Gripper jaws attachment; each file is one jaw, mirrored in the slicer for the other side.

Design File Use PETG body with a glued-on TPU pad MSG_JAW_TPU_GLUE the recommended jaw: the soft pad deforms around the object and holds it better Solid jaw MSG_solid_jaw, MSG_solid_jaw_mirror one part, quick to print Hollow jaw MSG_JAW_HOLLOW lighter, and suited to multi-colour prints Figure 13: The jaw body, with the mounting holes for the carrier.

docs.title: The TPU jaw
docs.text:
Figure 14: The TPU jaw: a PETG body (orange) and a TPU pad (green).

Print the body in PETG with your usual settings and the pad in TPU with 16 % infill, no top or bottom layers and two walls, for the softest pad. Then glue the pad to the body with ordinary super glue, in the orientation the pictures show: a pad glued the wrong way round leaves the jaws facing the wrong direction.

docs.title: Sponge pads
docs.text: A strip of 1 mm sponge tape (30 mm wide, in the BOM) on the gripping face of any jaw improves the hold on hard and smooth objects a great deal. Cut it to length, peel the backing and press it on.

docs.title: Your own jaws
docs.text: Keep the carrier's hole pattern from one of the designs and shape the rest for your objects. Long jaws multiply the lever arm on the carriers: keep them short and stiff, and remember that the grip force is set at the jaw faces, not at the rail.

docs.title: Calibrate after changing the jaws
docs.text: The gripper calibration finds the end stops with the jaws fitted; jaws that meet earlier or later than the old ones change where 255 is. Calibrate again after a change, which happens at the next power-up anyway.

docs.title: Mounting on a robot
docs.text: The gripper mounts by its coupler plate, the round plate on the back of the body behind the stepper. Two covers exist for it, and the STEP files let you make a third.

docs.title: An 8 mm shaft
docs.text:
As shipped, the coupler plate carries a shaft coupler with an 8 mm bore and M4 clamp screws under the ring_cover part: the gripper slides onto an 8 mm shaft and is clamped with the two M4 screws. Any robot or fixture that offers an 8 mm shaft takes the gripper this way.

Figure 9: The coupler plate with the 8 mm shaft coupler.

docs.title: PAROL6
docs.text:
For the PAROL6 wrist, replace ring_cover with ring_cover-PAROL6 from the STEP files (Common parts): it bolts to the robot's last joint. The PAROL6 gripper cable then runs from the gripper to the robot's gripper port; see The cable and On PAROL6 and PAR6.

Figure 10: The gripper with the PAROL6 ring cover (red).

docs.title: Another robot
docs.text: Adapt ring_cover, or the body itself, to your flange: the STEP files are open. Keep the gripper's connector reachable and the camera's view free, and route the cable so that it cannot be pulled by the robot's motion.

docs.title: On the bench
docs.text: For testing, clamp the body, not the jaws or the rail, and leave the whole stroke free: calibration moves the jaws from one end stop to the other without any command from you.

docs.title: First setup
docs.text:
From a mounted and cabled gripper to one that opens and closes on command. Motor GUI in the browser is the usual tool for it; every step also gives the Python call and the UART command.

  1. Motor GUI: the browser, the CANvas adapter, connecting to the gripper, the gripper panel.
  2. Calibrate, activate, move: the three things every session starts with, and the first grip.
  3. Driver configuration for a self-built gripper: what a bought gripper already has and a self-built one needs: the driver's motor calibration, gripper mode, the thermistor.

A gripper that has been through these pages is ready for Operation.

docs.title: Driver configuration for a self-built gripper
docs.text: A gripper from the shop arrives with its driver configured: the stepper calibrated, gripper mode on, the thermistor on, the gains set, everything saved. A gripper you build has a bare STEPFOC driver that must be brought to the same state once, over its UART port. This page is that procedure; the commands are the driver's, and the STEPFOC documentation explains each in depth.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• The driver mounted on the stepper with its encoder magnet, before the pinion is engaged in the racks: the motor calibration turns the motor several revolutions in both directions, which the racks cannot follow. Do this step with the stepper out of the gripper or with the pinion not yet fitted.
  • A 3.3 V USB-to-serial adapter on the driver's UART connector, a terminal at 256000 baud with CR+LF line endings, and 24 V on the driver's power connector. The serial terminal on the STEPFOC site shows the terminal setup.
  • The thermistor from the BOM, soldered to the driver's thermistor connector and placed in the motor's windings with thermal cement.

docs.title: With Motor GUI
docs.text: Motor GUI, connected over UART through the serial adapter, has a preset per stepper on its setup page: MSG 21.5 mm motor, MSG 40 mm motor and MSG 60 mm motor. A preset writes the stepper's resistance, inductance and 50 pole pairs, the current limit, the loop gains, gripper mode, the thermistor and the CAN ID, then saves; its CAN ID is 6, the PAR6 gripper's, so change it before applying for another robot. Apply it after the motor calibration of step 1: it does step 2 for you.

docs.title: 1. The motor calibration
docs.text:
Restore the defaults first, so that nothing from another motor or junk in the EEPROM goes into the calibration, then enter the stepper's parameters and calibrate:

Stepper #PP #R #L 21.5 mm, 17HS08-1004S 50 3.7 0.0045 40 mm, 17HS16-2004S1 50 1.1 0.0026 60 mm, 17HS24-2104S 50 1.6 0.0030 
#Default
#PP 50
#R 1.1
#L 0.0026
#Cal

The motor turns, the driver prints each step and ends with Calibration success!. The whole routine and its messages are in Calibration on the STEPFOC site. #Default also resets the serial number the driver reports; note what #Info printed if you need it.

docs.title: 2. The gripper settings
docs.text:
#Gripper 1
#Term 1
#Tlim 75
#Kpiq 1.4047
#Kiiq 0.1149
#CANID 0
#Save
Command What it does #Gripper 1 gripper mode: the driver runs the gripper state machine and answers the gripper messages #Term 1, #Tlim 75 the thermistor on, the temperature limit at 75 °C. Without it the motor can burn out under a long grip #Kpiq 1.4047, #Kiiq 0.1149 the current loop gains of Motor GUI's gripper presets, the same for the three steppers; the gains the calibration computes for the stepper are sharper than a gripper needs #CANID 0 the node ID on the robot's bus; 0 to 13, see Over CAN #Save nothing above survives a power cycle until it is saved

docs.title: 3. Assemble and calibrate the gripper
docs.text: Fit the pinion and assemble the gripper, power it up, and run the gripper calibration (#Gripcal, or Motor GUI's Calibrate): the jaws open fully and close fully. Then a first move at a low current, as in Calibrate, activate, move. #Gripinfo prints the gripper's state, including the end stops the calibration found.

docs.title: Current limit
docs.text: The gripper's moves use the current limit of each command, not the driver's #Ilim. Keep the commanded current at or below the stepper's maximum current (Force and speed); the firmware does not clamp it.

docs.title: Calibrate, activate, move
docs.text:
Every session with the gripper starts the same way: calibrate, activate, clear what errors there are. Then it moves. This page does it once with Motor GUI, with Python and over UART; How the gripper works explains what happens inside.

Danger

The jaws move over the whole stroke during calibration, and close with the set force afterwards. Nothing in reach of them, fingers included.

docs.title: 1. Power up
docs.text: At power-up the gripper reports Not calibrated and does not move. Its stepper must be calibrated too, which a bought gripper is from the factory; a self-built gripper gets that in Driver configuration.

docs.title: 2. Calibrate
docs.text:
The gripper calibration finds the two end stops: the jaws open fully, pause, then close fully, at low force (500 mA) and low speed. Each end is recognised when the jaws have stood still against it for half a second. It takes about ten seconds; the result is not kept over a power cycle, so this runs at every power-up.

Motor GUIPythonUART

Calibrate, and confirm. When the jaws stop, the panel shows Calibrated.

gripper.Send_gripper_calibrate()
time.sleep(10)

#Gripcal

If the jaws do not move at all, or move to one end and stop: the gripper is in an error state (clear it first, see step 4), or the stepper is not calibrated. If the routine runs for 24 seconds and gives up, an end stop was not found: something blocks the jaws short of the end, or the mechanism is too stiff for 500 mA.

docs.title: 3. Activate
docs.text:
A calibrated gripper carries out a move only while it is activated.

Motor GUIPythonUART

Activate. The panel shows Activated.

The activate bit is part of every move command (the fourth argument below); send it as 1.

#Grippos activates by itself; #Gripact 1 activates without moving.

docs.title: 4. Clear errors
docs.text:
The driver powers up in an error state until its motor is calibrated and it has run through its checks; an E-stop, an over-temperature or a supply fault leave an error too. A gripper with an error does not move.

Motor GUIPythonUART

Clear errors, when the panel shows an error.

gripper.Send_Clear_Error()

#Clear

An error whose cause is still present comes straight back; Errors and recovery says what each needs.

docs.title: 5. Move
docs.text:
A move is three numbers: the position (0 open, 255 closed), the speed (0 to 255) and the current limit in mA, which is the grip force (Force and speed). Start with speed 30 and 300 mA.

Motor GUIPythonUART

Set Speed 30 and Current 300 with their Set buttons, then Close and Open, or set a Position: the jaws follow, the plots show the position and the current, and the state says whether the jaws reached the position or stopped on something.

gripper.Send_gripper_data_pack(200, 30, 300, 1, 1, 0, 0)   # position, speed, current, activate, action, E-stop, release direction
time.sleep(2)
gripper.Send_gripper_data_pack(20, 30, 300, 1, 1, 0, 0)

#Gripvel 30
#Gripcur 300
#Grippos 200
#Grippos 20

Put an object between the jaws and close on it: the jaws stop on it and hold it with 300 mA, and the state reads object detected while closing. Raise the current for a firmer grip, within the stepper's rating, and the speed once the motion is what you want.

docs.title: What the gripper reports
docs.text: Every move command is answered with the gripper's state, which Motor GUI shows in its panel and the library puts into attributes: the position, the current, whether it is calibrated and activated, whether a move is in progress, the object-detection result, and the three error bits. How the gripper works goes through them.

docs.title: Motor GUI
docs.text:
Motor GUI is Source Robotics' tool for its drivers and for the grippers built on them: a page in the browser that reaches the hardware through the browser's serial port access, so there is nothing to install. With the CANvas adapter on the gripper's CAN bus it calibrates and activates the gripper, opens and closes it, shows its state and plots its position and current. It is the recommended tool for the first setup and for testing; everything it does is one CAN message, so what you learn here carries over to Python and the other interfaces.

The gripper GUI is legacy

The earlier SSG-gripper-GUI, a Python program with a Windows build, still works with both grippers but is not developed further. Use Motor GUI.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Chromium-based browser: Chrome, Edge, Brave or Opera. The serial port access Motor GUI relies on (Web Serial) is not in Firefox or Safari.
  • The CANvas adapter in a USB port and on the gripper's CAN bus, with the bus terminated (CAN termination), and the gripper powered.
  • Nothing on the gripper itself: a bought gripper is ready. The browser's port access and the adapter's installation are described on the STEPFOC site, Motor GUI.

docs.title: Connecting
docs.text:
1. Open motorgui.com. In the connection bar choose CAN (slcan) and the bitrate 1 Mbit/s, then connect: the browser asks which serial port, pick the CANvas adapter.
  2. Choose the gripper's node in the node picker: its CAN ID, 0 unless you changed it. Switch the bar from Motor to Gripper.
  3. The gripper panel fills in as soon as the gripper's feedback arrives: calibrated or not, activated or not, the position, the current and the errors. While it says that it is waiting for feedback, check the node ID, the power and that the driver is in gripper mode.

The panel works with one gripper at a time; to work with another on the same bus, pick its node. The Motor side of the switch shows the same driver as a motor, which the gripper does not need.

Try it without a gripper

The connection kind Mock CAN (demo) runs a simulated gripper in the browser: the whole panel, without an adapter or a gripper.

docs.title: The gripper panel
docs.text:
Control What it does Calibrate runs the gripper calibration: the jaws travel the whole stroke to find the end stops. The panel asks you to confirm; deactivate the gripper and take everything out of the jaws first Activate, Deactivate the activate bit: a calibrated gripper carries out moves only while it is activated Position, Speed, Current, each with Set the move: position 0 (open) to 255 (closed), speed 0 to 255, current limit 0 to 1500 mA, which is the force. Each Set sends its value together with the other two as last sent Open, Close a move to position 0 or 255 with the set speed and current Stop ends the move where the jaws are E-stop, or Esc stops the gripper at once: the move command with the E-stop bit, after which the gripper reports the E-stop error until it is cleared Clear errors clears the errors; an error whose cause remains comes straight back Plots position and current, live, with the requested position drawn in; the window and the scale are adjustable, and Export CSV saves a recorded run Events the feedback rate and the recent gripper events, with Export events for diagnostics Cycle test moves between two positions at a speed and a current, a number of times with a dwell: for endurance tests and demonstrations. Keep the tab visible while it runs

Motor GUI's current limit stops at 1500 mA. The 40 mm and 60 mm steppers take more (Force and speed); for their full force, command the move from Python or over CAN.

docs.title: Presets for a self-built gripper
docs.text: Connected over UART instead, through the serial adapter on the driver's UART port, Motor GUI's setup page has tuned presets for the grippers: MSG 21.5 mm motor, MSG 40 mm motor and MSG 60 mm motor, and SSG-48 for the other gripper. A preset writes the motor's parameters, the loop gains, gripper mode, the thermistor and the CAN ID to the driver and saves them; its CAN ID is 6, the PAR6 gripper's, so change it before applying for another robot. Driver configuration says when to apply it, and lists the same settings as commands for a terminal.

docs.title: What next
docs.text: Calibrate, activate, move is the first session with a connected gripper.

docs.title: Operation
docs.text: How a working gripper is used: what happens inside when it calibrates and moves, the interfaces it is driven through, and what to do when it reports an error.

docs.title: Over CAN
docs.text: CAN is the gripper's interface: the one cable carries it next to the power, and a robot's control board, a PC with the CANvas adapter or any microcontroller with a CAN transceiver drives the gripper with it. The gripper is a STEPFOC driver on the bus, so the frames are the driver's; this page is the part a gripper needs.

docs.title: The frame
docs.text:
CAN 2.0 data frames with 11-bit identifiers at 1 Mbit/s. The identifier carries the node, the command and the error state:

Figure 16: Bits 10 to 7 of the identifier are the node ID, bits 6 to 1 the command ID, bit 0 the error bit.
  • Node ID, bits 10 to 7: which device. Every gripper ships as node 0; set another with Send_CAN_ID or #CANID and save it. Use 0 to 13: the driver's bootloader reserves 14 and 15, and a device on one of those cannot be updated over CAN.
  • Command ID, bits 6 to 1: which message. The gripper command is 61, its answer 60, the calibration 62.
  • Error bit, bit 0: in a frame from the gripper, 1 while any error is active. In a frame from the host it is ignored.

So the gripper command to node 0 travels on identifier (0 << 7) | (61 << 1) = 0x7A, and the answer comes back on (60 << 1) | error = 0x78 or 0x79; to node 3 the command is 0x1FA and the answer 0x1F8. Multi-byte values are big-endian; flags inside a byte are numbered from the most significant bit.

docs.title: The messages a gripper needs
docs.text:
Message ID What for Send_gripper_data_pack 61 the move command: position, speed, current, the activate, action and E-stop bits; 0 bytes to poll Respond_Gripper_data_pack 60 the answer: position, current, the state and error bits Send_gripper_calibrate 62 the gripper calibration, after every power-up Send_Clear_Error 1 clears the errors Send_ESTOP, Send_Idle 0, 12 stop Send_Watchdog 15 the gripper stops when the host stops talking Send_CAN_ID, Send_Save_config 11, 13 another node ID, saved Send_Respond_State_of_Errors, Send_Respond_Temperature 26, 23 the driver's error flags, the motor temperature

The CAN reference has the bytes of each; the driver's other messages, which a gripper does not need, are on the STEPFOC site.

docs.title: A control loop
docs.text:
1. At power-up: Send_Clear_Error, then Send_gripper_calibrate; poll with empty Send_gripper_data_pack frames until the calibrated bit is 1 (about ten seconds).
  2. For each grip: one Send_gripper_data_pack with the position, speed and current and the activate and action bits set; then poll with empty frames until the object-detection field reads 1, 2 or 3, or your own timeout passes.
  3. Keep polling at a steady rate (50 Hz is plenty) if you set the watchdog: every frame resets it, and the gripper stops by itself when your program stops.

The answer to every frame tells the whole state, so a host never has to ask twice.

docs.title: From a PC
docs.text: The CANvas adapter shows up as a serial port and speaks slcan; python-can opens it with bustype='slcan', and the Python library wraps the messages. Any CAN adapter that python-can supports works the same way.

docs.title: On a bus with other devices
docs.text: A gripper on a robot shares the bus with the robot's joints or other grippers. Give each device its own node ID (connect one at a time, Send_CAN_ID, Send_Save_config), terminate both ends of the bus (CAN termination), and keep in mind that a lower node ID wins the bus arbitration.

docs.title: Errors and recovery
docs.text: When the driver inside the gripper detects a fault it stops the motor, goes to idle and sets the error bit in every CAN frame it sends. The grip is released: an idle stepper holds nothing beyond the mechanism's friction.

docs.title: Seeing the error
docs.text:
• The error bit of every answer's identifier: 1 while any error is active.
  • Respond_Gripper_data_pack carries the three gripper error bits: temperature, timeout, E-stop.
  • Send_Respond_State_of_Errors returns every flag of the driver, which is where the other causes show.
  • Motor GUI shows the errors in its gripper panel; #Error over UART prints them.

docs.title: The errors
docs.text:
Error Reported in Cause What to do Temperature the gripper's temperature bit the thermistor in the windings reads more than 75 °C (#Tlim) let the motor cool; hold with less current Timeout the gripper's timeout bit the driver's CAN watchdog ran out: no valid frame within the time set by Send_Watchdog the host stopped sending; fix the host, then clear E-stop the gripper's E-stop bit a move command with the E-stop bit set, or #Gripstop 1 clear, then send a command with the bit at 0: a command with the bit still set raises it again Not calibrated (motor) State_of_Errors, #Error the driver's own motor calibration is missing: a self-built gripper before Driver configuration, or after #Default calibrate the motor Vbus State_of_Errors the supply is below 9 V or above 29.5 V the supply, the cable Encoder State_of_Errors the driver's encoder does not see its magnet the magnet on the stepper shaft (a self-built gripper) Driver State_of_Errors the driver stage's own protection tripped: overcurrent, overtemperature lower the current; check the motor leads Velocity State_of_Errors the motor exceeded the driver's speed limit unlikely in a gripper; clear Driver E-stop State_of_Errors Send_ESTOP was received clear

A gripper that is not gripper-calibrated is not in error: it just refuses moves until Send_gripper_calibrate has found the end stops.

docs.title: Clearing
docs.text:
Send_Clear_Error, Clear in the GUI or #Clear clears every flag, the gripper's E-stop included, and goes to idle. An error whose cause is still present comes straight back: a hot motor, a supply that is still low. After an E-stop, the next move command must carry the E-stop bit at 0, or the error is raised again at once.

After clearing, the gripper is idle and still calibrated and activated; the next move command moves it.

docs.title: When the gripper does not answer
docs.text:
• No answer at all: the supply, the cable (and its pinout), the bus termination (about 60 Ω across CANH and CANL with everything unpowered), 1 Mbit/s on the adapter, the node ID.
  • Answers but does not move: not calibrated, not activated, an error active, or the action bit at 0.
  • Moves to one end during calibration and stops there: the other end stop is blocked, or the mechanism is too stiff for the calibration's 500 mA; after 24 seconds the routine gives up.

Troubleshooting goes through the symptoms one by one.

docs.title: How the gripper works
docs.text: The gripper is a state machine in the driver's firmware, fed by one command and answering with one status. This page is what it does with them.

docs.title: The states
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> NotCalibrated: power-up
    NotCalibrated --> Calibrating: Send_gripper_calibrate / #Gripcal
    Calibrating --> Calibrated: both end stops found
    Calibrating --> NotCalibrated: 24 s without an end stop
    Calibrated --> Moving: command with activate = 1, action = 1
    Moving --> Holding: object found, or position reached
    Holding --> Moving: a different command
    Moving --> Idle: error, E-stop, action = 0
    Holding --> Idle: error, E-stop, action = 0
    Idle --> Moving: command, errors cleared

Not calibrated. After power-up the gripper does not know where its jaws are. It answers status requests and refuses moves. The gripper calibration is not kept over a power cycle.

Calibrating. The jaws open at speed 40 and 500 mA until they have stood still against the end stop for half a second, pause briefly, then close the same way. The two positions become 0 and 255. If an end stop is not found within 24 seconds, the routine gives up and the gripper stays uncalibrated. Nothing else is accepted while it runs; the action bit of the status reads 0.

Moving. A command with the activate and action bits set starts a move towards the position, at the speed, with the current limited to the commanded value. The driver runs its velocity loop towards the target and watches two things: the speed of the jaws and the motor current.

Holding. The move ends in one of two ways. The jaws reach the target (within 5 encoder ticks) and the driver switches to position control and holds it there: object detection reads 3. Or the jaws stop before the target with the current at its limit: an object is in the way, and the driver keeps pushing with the limited current, which is the grip. Object detection reads 1 if the jaws were closing, 2 if they were opening. Nothing moves until a different command arrives.

Idle. An error, the E-stop bit, or a command with the action bit at 0 takes the gripper to idle: the motor is no longer driven and holds nothing beyond the mechanism's friction, so an object can slip. Clearing the error, or the next command with the action bit set, moves it again.

docs.title: The command
docs.text:
Send_gripper_data_pack carries, in 5 bytes:

Field Range Meaning Position 0 to 255 0 fully open, 255 fully closed, linear over the stroke Speed 0 to 255 500 to 60000 encoder ticks per second, see Force and speed Current mA the current limit of the move, so the grip force; not clamped by the firmware Activate bit 1 activates the gripper; 0 deactivates it, and it stops Action bit 1 carries out the move; 0 stores the command and leaves the gripper idle E-stop bit 1 stops the gripper and raises the E-stop error Release direction bit read by the firmware but not used

The same command sent twice does nothing new: the driver compares every command with the previous one, and only a changed command resets the "at position" state and starts a move. So a host may repeat the command at any rate, which the CAN watchdog needs; to move the jaws from a held position to the same position again, change the speed or the current by one.

An empty Send_gripper_data_pack, 0 bytes, changes nothing and is answered like a full one: it is the status poll, and it costs the bus almost nothing. A host usually sends one full command per move and polls with empty ones.

Over UART, #Grippos is the same command: it sets the position, activates the gripper, sets the action bit and starts the move, with the speed and current last set by #Gripvel and #Gripcur (50 and 400 mA after power-up).

docs.title: The answer
docs.text:
Every Send_gripper_data_pack is answered with Respond_Gripper_data_pack, 4 bytes:

Field Meaning Position where the jaws are, 0 to 255 Current the motor current, mA; positive while opening, negative while closing Activated the activate flag Action status 1 while a move is in progress, 0 when idle, holding, or calibrating Object detection 0 moving, 1 object found while closing, 2 object found while opening, 3 at the position Temperature error the motor's thermistor is above the limit Timeout error the driver's CAN watchdog ran out E-stop error the E-stop bit was received Calibrated the gripper calibration is done

The bits are listed in Errors and status bits, with the byte layout in the CAN reference.

docs.title: Object detection, exactly
docs.text:
While a move is in progress and the jaws are not yet at the target, the driver reads moving (0) as long as the jaws move faster than 500 encoder ticks per second, about 1.6 mm/s. When they are slower than that and the motor current is above 80 % of the commanded limit, something stops them: object found, 1 or 2 by the sign of the current. Below 80 % with the jaws slow, it still reads moving: the jaws are accelerating or the object is soft and still being squeezed. Once the target is reached, 3, and it stays 3 until a different command arrives.

The state is therefore a snapshot of each answer. A host that wants to know "did the grip succeed" sends the move, then polls until the state is 1, 2 or 3, with a timeout of its own; the ROS 2 driver and the PAROL6 software do exactly that.

docs.title: What the current limit does
docs.text: The current limit of a move is the driver's Iq limit for the duration of the move and the hold. It bounds the torque, so the force on an object, and it also bounds how fast the jaws accelerate: a low limit with a high speed gives a gentle, slow-starting move. The temperature of the motor is the other bound: holding an object at a high current for minutes heats the windings, and at 75 °C the thermistor stops the gripper.

docs.title: Timing
docs.text: The driver runs its loops at 6250 Hz; a move command takes effect at the next cycle, and the answer leaves within a millisecond. The CAN bus at 1 Mbit/s carries a command and its answer in well under half a millisecond, so a host can run the gripper at several hundred commands per second; 50 Hz is a good rate for a controller that polls the state.

docs.title: With Python
docs.text: The Spectral-BLDC library wraps the driver's CAN protocol, gripper messages included: one method per message, and the gripper's answers unpacked into attributes. The ROS 2 driver and the legacy gripper GUI are built on it.

docs.title: Installing
docs.text:
pip install Spectral-BLDC

The source and the examples are in Spectral-BLDC-Python.

docs.title: The first program
docs.text:
import Spectral_BLDC as Spectral
import time

# the adapter: a CANvas on COM20 (Windows) or /dev/ttyACM0 (Linux), 1 Mbit/s
bus = Spectral.CanCommunication(bustype='slcan', channel='COM20', bitrate=1000000)
gripper = Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=0, communication=bus)

gripper.Send_Clear_Error()
gripper.Send_gripper_calibrate()
time.sleep(10)                                  # the jaws open fully, then close fully

for position in (200, 20, 200, 20):
    # position 0..255, speed 0..255, current mA, activate, action, E-stop, release direction
    gripper.Send_gripper_data_pack(position, 30, 300, 1, 1, 0, 0)
    for _ in range(40):                         # poll the state for up to 2 s
        gripper.Send_gripper_data_pack()        # an empty frame: status only
        message, ids = bus.receive_can_messages(timeout=0.05)
        if message is not None:
            gripper.UnpackData(message, ids)
            print(gripper.gripper_position, gripper.gripper_current, gripper.gripper_object_detection)
            if gripper.gripper_object_detection in (1, 2, 3):   # object found, or at the position
                break

Send_gripper_data_pack with all seven arguments sends the move; without arguments it sends the empty status poll. receive_can_messages returns the raw python-can message and the node ID, command ID and error bit from the identifier; UnpackData fills the gripper attributes:

Attribute Meaning gripper_position 0 open to 255 closed gripper_current the motor current in mA gripper_activated, gripper_action_status the activate flag; 1 while a move is in progress gripper_object_detection 0 moving, 1 object found while closing, 2 object found while opening, 3 at the position gripper_temperature_error, gripper_timeout_error, gripper_estop_error the three error bits gripper_calibrated the gripper calibration is done

Object detection in library 1.20

Library version 1.20 assembles gripper_object_detection with its two bits swapped relative to the firmware: it reports 1 where the gripper sends 2 (object found while opening) and 2 where it sends 1 (object found while closing); 0 and 3 are unaffected. Until the library is fixed, swap the two values in your program, or test for "1 or 2" as this example does.

docs.title: Stopping
docs.text:
gripper.Send_gripper_data_pack(20, 30, 300, 1, 1, 1, 0)   # the E-stop bit: stops, raises the E-stop error
gripper.Send_Clear_Error()                                 # clears it; the next command must have the bit at 0
gripper.Send_Watchdog(500)                                 # from now on the gripper stops 500 ms after the last frame

With the watchdog set, keep the status poll running at a steady rate; a program that crashes releases the grip within the watchdog time.

docs.title: Several grippers
docs.text:
One CanCommunication per bus, one SpectralCAN per gripper with its node ID; every answer carries the node ID in ids.node_id, so route it to the right object. The teleoperation guide couples two grippers this way.

The complete map of calls to messages is in the Python library reference.

docs.title: On PAROL6 and PAR6
docs.text: The gripper is made for the Source Robotics arms. Both drive it over their own CAN bus; their software calibrates it, moves it and reads its state, so a program for the robot does not talk CAN itself.

docs.title: PAROL6
docs.text:
1. Mount the gripper with the ring_cover-PAROL6 part (Mounting on a robot).
  2. Connect it with the PAROL6 gripper cable to the robot's gripper port. Only this cable: the PAR6 cable is wired differently and destroys the gripper (The cable).
  3. Leave the gripper's node ID at 0 and its termination switch ON; it is the last node on the robot's bus.

The PAROL6 commander software has the electric gripper's controls: calibrate, then a position, a speed and a current for a move, and the gripper's status. The PAROL6 Python API does the same from a program:

from robot_api import control_electric_gripper, get_electric_gripper_status

control_electric_gripper(action="calibrate")
control_electric_gripper(action="move", position=100, speed=150, current=200)
print(get_electric_gripper_status())

The PAROL6 documentation covers the robot's side: the gripper port, the commander software and the API.

docs.title: PAR6
docs.text: The PAR6 arm's control box runs the gripper on its CAN bus as a tool, with the PAR6 gripper cable (different from the PAROL6 one). The PAR6 documentation covers the tool configuration, the runtime's gripper commands and the firmware updates the box can do for the gripper.

docs.title: Another robot
docs.text: Any controller with a CAN interface drives the gripper directly: Over CAN is the protocol, With Python and With ROS 2 are two ready implementations, and the CAN reference has every byte.

docs.title: With ROS 2
docs.text: The msg_gripper_ros2 package is a ROS 2 Humble driver for the gripper, built on the Python library and a python-can adapter. It was developed by the UCLA Biomechatronics Lab and Ben Forbes, and is MIT licensed.

docs.title: What it offers
docs.text: Direction Topic or action Type Command /gripper/command_joint_states sensor_msgs/JointState, the position as the gripper's own units, 0 to 255 Feedback /gripper/feedback_joint_states sensor_msgs/JointState, the position in the same units and the effort in mA Action /gripper_command control_msgs/GripperCommand

docs.title: Installing
docs.text:
Ubuntu 22.04 with ROS 2 Humble, Python 3.10 or newer, and a USB-to-CAN adapter that speaks slcan, such as the CANvas:

pip install Spectral_BLDC python-can
cd ~/ros2_ws/src
git clone https://github.com/Source-Robotics/source_robotics_msg_gripper_ros2.git
cd ~/ros2_ws
colcon build --packages-select msg_gripper_ros2
source install/setup.bash

On Linux, add yourself to the dialout group to open the adapter's port without sudo, and log in again.

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
ros2 launch msg_gripper_ros2 msg_gripper_launch.py

The only setting that depends on your machine is the adapter's port, channel in config/default.yaml: /dev/ttyACM0 or /dev/ttyUSB0 on Linux, /dev/tty.usbmodem* on macOS, COM3 on Windows. Copy the file, change it, and pass it at launch:

ros2 launch msg_gripper_ros2 msg_gripper_launch.py config_file:=~/my_gripper.yaml node_name:=my_gripper namespace:=robot

The package's README has the rest: the parameters, the node names, and the platforms it was tested on.

docs.title: The SSG-48 package
docs.text: The ssg48_adaptive_electric_gripper_ros2 package, written for the SSG-48 gripper, speaks the same protocol and should work with the MSG as well.

docs.title: The description files
docs.text: The URDF and the MJCF of the gripper for ROS 2, Gazebo and MuJoCo are in the product repository's MSG_gripper_description.

docs.title: Over UART
docs.text: The driver inside the gripper has a serial port. It is not the gripper's everyday interface, which is CAN, but it is the way to configure the driver of a self-built gripper and the quickest way to look at what the driver reports when something is wrong.

docs.title: Reaching the port
docs.text:
The UART connector of the driver (JST SH, 4 pins, 3.3 V) is inside the housing, under the coupler plate. Unscrew the plate, plug in the USB-to-serial adapter with the UART cable, and open a terminal at 256000 baud with CR+LF line endings; the gripper's 24 V must be on for anything but reading settings. The serial terminal on the STEPFOC site walks through the terminal setup.

Danger

The port is 3.3 V. A 5 V adapter destroys the driver.

docs.title: The gripper commands
docs.text:
Command What it does #Gripper 1 gripper mode on (set and saved on every gripper); #Gripper prints it #Gripcal the gripper calibration #Gripvel 30 the speed of the next moves, 0 to 255 #Gripcur 300 the current limit of the next moves, mA #Grippos 200 move to the position, 0 open to 255 closed; activates the gripper and starts the move #Gripact 1 the activate flag without moving #Gripstop 1 the E-stop bit #Gripinfo the gripper's state: calibrated, activated, the setpoints, the object detection, the end stops

Only #Grippos starts a move. A session:

#Clear
#Gripcal
#Gripinfo
#Gripvel 30
#Gripcur 300
#Grippos 200
#Grippos 20

The UART reference has these and the driver commands a gripper needs; the driver's whole command set is on the STEPFOC site.

docs.title: Firmware release notes
docs.text: What changed in each release of the STEPFOC firmware the gripper runs, from the release notes in the driver's repository, up to the release this site describes. Entries about the driver's motion modes do not concern a gripper; the gripper mode, the CAN protocol and the bootloader do.

docs.title: V108 (2026-08-26)
docs.text: STEPFOC firmware V108 — application image for flashing via the Spectral bootloader.

docs.title: Bug fixes
docs.text:
• Fixed calibration (#Cal) spuriously failing with Phase order is wrong! on otherwise-healthy motors. The "confirm commutation" pre-check (before the real angle-offset search) commands a pure torque-axis voltage using the not-yet-calibrated encoder angle — depending on a given unit's actual rotor-to-encoder mounting angle, that command could land almost entirely on the wrong axis and produce ~zero torque, failing the check even though nothing was actually broken. Bench-confirmed on a real unit.
  • Fix: retry the pre-check once at a 90° angle bias before declaring failure — guaranteed to land within 45° of the true torque axis on at least one of the two tries. The downstream angle-offset search is unaffected and already independent of this pre-check.
  • Added Spin-confirm delta / Vbus diagnostics to #Cal's failure report, for the rare case both tries still fail.

docs.title: V107 (2026-08-24)
docs.text: STEPFOC firmware V107 — application image for flashing via the Spectral bootloader.

docs.title: Bug fixes
docs.text: • Fixed PD mode (IN_DATA_PACK_PD over CAN): the commanded speed was written into Feedforward_speed, but PD_mode() reads Velocity_setpoint for its KD term — so the KD (velocity-damping) term of the impedance controller was always evaluated against a stale/zero setpoint and had no effect. The CAN handler now writes the field the control law actually reads. IN_DATA_PACK_1 / position mode is unaffected — Feedforward_speed there is correct and continues to feed the position cascade.

docs.title: CAN bus
docs.text:
• Added a generic settings command (IN_SETTINGS) so future boolean settings don't each need their own command ID. Payload is mask + value (one byte each), one bit per setting — only bits set in the mask are applied, so a sender only needs to know about the bits it cares about.
  • First setting on this command: brake vs. coast (bit 0), previously only selectable over UART (Brake / Coast), now selectable over CAN as well.
