docs.title: V106 (2026-07-05)
docs.text: STEPFOC firmware V106 — application image for flashing via the Spectral bootloader.

docs.title: CAN bus
docs.text:
• The controller now drains up to 8 CAN messages per pass instead of just 1, so short bursts (multiple commands sent back-to-back, or a busy multi-node bus) no longer silently drop messages once the 3-deep hardware FIFO fills.
  • A CAN peripheral that fails to initialize no longer bricks the board — UART stays fully usable, only the CAN bus is skipped.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
• Added a hardware watchdog (100ms). If the control loop ever stops running, the board resets instead of leaving the motor driven at a stale duty cycle.
  • Fixed a bug where Torque_mode could silently overwrite your commanded Iq setpoint when clamping to the current limit — reading it back after clamping now shows what you actually asked for, and raising the current limit afterward immediately restores the original commanded torque instead of requiring the command to be resent.
  • Fixed undefined behavior in a serial-protocol integer conversion (fourBytesToInt).
  • Synced default configuration values that had drifted between two locations in the code, so a fresh #Default and a freshly-flashed board's built-in defaults now agree.

docs.title: EEPROM / configuration integrity
docs.text:
• Added CRC validation over the saved configuration, split into two independent halves: calibration data (resistance, inductance, Kt/KV, angle offset, current-loop gains, etc.) and settings (PID tuning, limits, watchdog config, CAN ID, etc.).
  • This means a corrupted save (e.g. from a power loss mid-write) is detected and safely defaulted instead of silently running with garbage values — and critically, a future firmware update that only adds a new setting can no longer wipe your calibration, since the two are validated independently.
  • Boards upgrading from older, pre-CRC firmware keep their existing calibration automatically — no need to recalibrate after this update.
  • A few unused slots were reserved in the calibration block for upcoming features (e.g. magnet alignment), so those can be added later without another migration.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
• PWM output no longer re-resolves which timer/channel it's writing to on every single call (it was doing this 4x per control tick) — resolved once and cached, freeing up ISR headroom.
  • Velocity calculation switched from a floating-point divide to an integer multiply.

docs.title: Usability
docs.text:

Worked examples around the gripper.

  • Teleoperation with two grippers: one gripper follows the other and pushes back what it feels, over one CAN bus and a few lines of Python.

docs.title: Basic control in Python
docs.text:
The shortest program that drives the gripper: it connects through the CANvas adapter, clears the errors, calibrates, then closes and opens every three seconds and prints what the gripper answers. It is the example from the product repository's README; pip install Spectral-BLDC is the only requirement. Change COM20 to your adapter's port (/dev/ttyACM0 on Linux) and node_id to the gripper's CAN ID if you changed it from 0.

Danger

700 mA closes the jaws with real force, about 14 N with the 21.5 mm stepper and 25 N with the 60 mm. Keep fingers out of the jaws, and start with a lower current if the gripper is new to you.

import Spectral_BLDC as Spectral
import time

Communication1 = Spectral.CanCommunication(bustype='slcan', channel='COM20', bitrate=1000000)
Motor1 = Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=0, communication=Communication1)

Motor1.Send_Clear_Error()
Motor1.Send_gripper_calibrate()
time.sleep(4)

temp_var = 0
while True:
   if temp_var == 0:
      Motor1.Send_gripper_data_pack(50,100,700,1,1,0,0)
      temp_var = 1
   elif temp_var == 1:
      Motor1.Send_gripper_data_pack(240,100,700,1,1,0,0)
      temp_var = 0

   message, UnpackedMessageID = Communication1.receive_can_messages(timeout=0.2)

   if message is not None:
      print(f"Message is: {message}")
      print(f"Node ID is : {UnpackedMessageID.node_id}")
      print(f"Message ID is: {UnpackedMessageID.command_id}")
      print(f"Error bit is: {UnpackedMessageID.error_bit}")
      print(f"Timestamp is: {message.timestamp}")

   time.sleep(3)

The arguments of Send_gripper_data_pack, in order: the position (0 open, 255 closed), the speed (0 to 255), the current limit in mA (the force), then the activate bit, the action bit, the E-stop bit and the release direction. With Python explains the library's calls, How the gripper works the state the gripper answers with, and Force and speed what the current means in newtons.

docs.title: Teleoperation with two grippers
docs.text:
Two grippers on one CAN bus, coupled so that each follows the other: squeeze one by hand and the other closes; when the other meets an object, the one in your hand pushes back with the force it feels. A hundred lines of Python, and the basis of a teleoperation setup with force feedback.

This guide does not use the gripper mode. Both drivers run in current (torque) mode, the driver's own motion command, and the PC closes a position loop between them at a fixed rate. The gripper mode's position, speed and object detection are not involved; the drivers are plain torque sources here.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Two grippers, calibrated as motors (a bought gripper is), with different node IDs: 0 and 1 (#CANID 1, #Save on one of them over UART).
  • Both on one bus with the CANvas adapter, 24 V on both, termination at the two ends.
  • pip install Spectral-BLDC SourceRoboticsToolbox.

Warning

In current mode the gripper has no end-stop knowledge and no object detection: it pushes with whatever current the loop commands. Set the driver's current limit to the stepper's rating (#Ilim) on both grippers, start with low gains, and keep fingers out of the jaws.

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
Each driver is commanded a current proportional to the difference between the two positions, plus a damping term on the speed difference and a little damping of its own motion:

\[ I_0 = K_p\,(p_1 - p_0) + K_d\,(v_1 - v_0) - K_k\, v_0, \qquad I_1 = K_p\,(p_0 - p_1) + K_d\,(v_0 - v_1) - K_k\, v_1 \]

\(p\) is the jaw position of each gripper in the same units, \(v\) its speed. When the two positions agree, both currents are zero and the grippers rest. Move one by hand and the difference drives the other after it; block the other, and the difference drives the one in your hand back with the same current, which is the force you feel. \(K_p\) is the stiffness of the virtual spring between them, \(K_d\) its damping.

The two drivers' encoders do not read the same number at the same jaw position, so each position is referred to a reference reading taken once with both grippers in the same position; the Source Robotics Toolbox's Joint does that bookkeeping and unwraps the encoder over its 16384-tick turns.

docs.title: The code
docs.text:
import time
import numpy as np
import Spectral_BLDC as Spectral
import SourceRoboticsToolbox as Toolbox

INTERVAL_S = 0.002                 # the loop rate: 500 Hz
REFERENCE = [10440, 13555]         # each gripper's raw encoder reading with both jaws in the same position

Kp, Kd, Kk = 650, 0.0055, 0.0003   # stiffness, damping between the two, damping of each

bus = Spectral.CanCommunication(bustype='slcan', channel='COM123', bitrate=1000000)
motors = [Spectral.SpectralCAN(node_id=i, communication=bus) for i in (0, 1)]
joints = [Toolbox.Joint(encoder_resolution=14, master_position=REFERENCE[i], gear_ratio=1, offset=0, dir=0)
          for i in (0, 1)]

position = np.zeros(2)             # each gripper's position, referred to its reference
sector_known = [False, False]
current = [0, 0]

while True:
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for i in (0, 1):               # command the currents; each answer carries position and speed
        motors[i].Send_data_pack_1(Position=None, Speed=None, Current=int(current[i]))
    for _ in (0, 1):
        message, ids = bus.receive_can_messages(timeout=0.001)
        if ids is None:
            continue
        i = ids[0]
        motors[i].UnpackData(message, ids)
        if not sector_known[i]:
            joints[i].determine_sector(motors[i].position)
            sector_known[i] = True
        position[i] = joints[i].get_joint_position(motors[i].position)

    current[0] = Kp * (position[1] - position[0]) + Kd * (motors[1].speed - motors[0].speed) - Kk * motors[0].speed
    current[1] = Kp * (position[0] - position[1]) + Kd * (motors[0].speed - motors[1].speed) - Kk * motors[1].speed

    time.sleep(max(0.0, INTERVAL_S - (time.perf_counter() - t0)))

The reference readings: with both grippers powered and their jaws set by hand to the same opening, read each driver's position (#Info over UART, or Send_Respond_Encoder_data from Python) and put the two numbers in REFERENCE.

docs.title: Tuning
docs.text:
Start with Kp at a tenth of the value above and raise it until the follower tracks the leader without lagging; raise Kd if the pair oscillates. The current the formula produces is in mA and is clamped by each driver's #Ilim, so the stepper's rating is the ceiling of the force feedback. A fixed loop rate matters: a loop that runs at an uneven rate makes the damping terms noisy.

The full example, with a timer for a precise loop rate, is gripper_teleop_PC_calc.py in the Python library's examples, and the bilateral teleoperation guide on the STEPFOC site explains the control law with a joint instead of a gripper.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text:
The gripper's CAN messages and UART commands, its status and error bits, and the Python library calls that send them, for the firmware named on the landing page. The gripper is a STEPFOC stepper driver in gripper mode and accepts the driver's whole command set; only what a gripper host or a self-built gripper needs is here, the rest is in the STEPFOC reference.

  • CAN messages: the identifier, and the gripper, system and status messages
  • UART commands: the gripper commands, the driver setup commands, status and utility
  • Errors and status bits
  • Python library: which library call sends which message

Conventions. Bytes are numbered from 0 and multi-byte values are big-endian. Bits are numbered from the most significant: bit 7 is the first flag in a byte. The position is 0 (open) to 255 (closed), the speed 0 to 255, the current in mA. UART command names are case-sensitive.

The command IDs, frame lengths and responses are read from the firmware's source at its release tag when the site is built, so they cannot drift from the firmware; the descriptions and byte layouts are written by hand.

docs.title: The gripper's state byte
docs.text:
Byte 3 of Respond_Gripper_data_pack, the answer to every gripper command, bits numbered from the most significant:

Bit Flag Meaning 7 activated the activate flag is set 6 action_status 1 while a move is in progress; 0 when idle, holding, auto-releasing or calibrating 5, 4 object_detection bit 5 is the low bit, bit 4 the high bit: 0 moving, 1 object found while closing, 2 object found while opening, 3 at the position 3 temperature_error the thermistor in the windings is above the limit 2 timeout_error the driver's CAN watchdog ran out 1 estop_error the E-stop bit of a command was received 0 calibrated the gripper calibration is done

The Python library's attributes are gripper_activated, gripper_action_status, gripper_object_detection, gripper_temperature_error, gripper_timeout_error, gripper_estop_error and gripper_calibrated; library version 1.20 assembles gripper_object_detection with its two bits swapped (1 and 2 exchanged).

docs.title: The driver's error flags
docs.text:
The flags as the firmware keeps them, the line #Error prints for each, and where each sits in the two bytes of Send_Respond_State_of_Errors (bits numbered from the most significant).

Flag #Error prints Byte, bit Raised when Error In error state! 0, 7 any of the flags below is set (also the error bit of every CAN identifier) temperature_error Temp error 0, 6 the thermistor reads above #Tlim (75 °C) encoder_error Encoder error 0, 5 the driver's encoder does not see its magnet Vbus_error Vbus error 0, 4 the supply is below 9 V or above 29.5 V Driver_error Driver error (undervoltage, thermal shutdown, or overcurrent) 0, 3 the driver stage's fault output is active Velocity_error Velocity error 0, 2 the motor speed exceeds the driver's limit Current_error Current error 0, 1 never in this firmware; reserved ESTOP_error Received ESTOP command 0, 0 Send_ESTOP was received Calibrated (0) Not calibrated 1, 7 (1 = calibrated) the driver's motor calibration is missing Activated — 1, 6 the activated flag, not an error Watchdog_error Watchdog error 1, 5 the watchdog time passed without a valid CAN frame

The gripper's timeout_error is the driver's Watchdog_error; the gripper's temperature_error is the driver's. The gripper's estop_error is its own, raised by the E-stop bit of the gripper command, and is distinct from the driver's ESTOP_error raised by Send_ESTOP.

docs.title: Clearing
docs.text: Send_Clear_Error and #Clear clear every flag, the gripper's E-stop included, and go to idle; a flag whose cause persists is set again at once. After an E-stop, the next gripper command must carry the E-stop bit at 0. The driver's Calibrated flag is set only by the motor calibration (#Cal).

docs.title: The LED
docs.text: The driver's status LED is inside the housing: three short flashes and a pause in normal operation, flashing every 0.5 s during the motor calibration, on steadily in error mode or while the motor is not calibrated.

docs.title: Python library
docs.text: The Spectral-BLDC package (Spectral-BLDC-Python, pip install Spectral-BLDC) has one method per CAN message in Spectral_BLDC.SpectralCAN, and Spectral_BLDC.CanCommunication for the bus. With Python shows how they are used with the gripper.

Send_gripper_data_pack(position, speed, current, activate, action, estop, release_direction) sends the 5-byte move; called without arguments it sends the empty frame that only asks for the state.

docs.title: Receiving
docs.text:
CanCommunication.receive_can_messages(timeout) returns (message, ids): the raw python-can message and a tuple ids with node_id, command_id and error_bit from the identifier, or (None, None) after the timeout. SpectralCAN.UnpackData(message, ids) decodes the message into the object's attributes:

Message Attributes Respond_Gripper_data_pack gripper_position, gripper_current, gripper_activated, gripper_action_status, gripper_object_detection, gripper_temperature_error, gripper_timeout_error, gripper_estop_error, gripper_calibrated Send_Respond_State_of_Errors error, temperature_error, encoder_error, vbus_error, driver_error, velocity_error, current_error, estop_error, calibrated, activated, watchdog_error Send_Respond_Temperature temperature Send_Respond_Voltage voltage Send_Respond_Device_Info HARDWARE_VERSION, BATCH_DATE, SOFTWARE_VERSION, SERIAL_NUMBER

Object detection in the library

Library version 1.20 assembles gripper_object_detection with the two bits swapped relative to the firmware, so it reports 1 where the gripper sends 2 (object detected while opening) and 2 where it sends 1 (object detected while closing); 0 and 3 are unaffected. Until the library is fixed, swap the two values in your program, or read the bits yourself from the frame.

docs.title: CAN messages
docs.text:
CAN 2.0, 1 Mbit/s, 11-bit identifiers. The identifier carries the node ID (bits 10 to 7, 0 to 13), the command ID (bits 6 to 1, 0 to 63) and, in frames from the gripper, the error bit (bit 0). Over CAN explains how the pieces are used; this page lists them.

Three kinds of message:

  • Send_… — the host sends data to the gripper. The gripper command is answered with Respond_Gripper_data_pack; the others are not answered.
  • Send_Respond_… — the host asks for data with a remote frame (RTR bit set, no data) under the command ID; the gripper answers with a data frame under the same command ID.
  • Respond_… — frames only the gripper sends.

Multi-byte values are big-endian (data[0] first); bits inside a byte are numbered from the most significant bit (bit 7 first).

docs.title: Send_gripper_data_pack
docs.text:
ID 61host → driver0 or 5 bytesPython: Send_gripper_data_pack()

The gripper command, for a driver set up as a gripper (#Gripper 1, saved). Position, speed and the current limit of the move, plus the activate, action and E-stop bits. A move is carried out only while the gripper is calibrated, activated and the action bit is 1. An empty frame (0 bytes) only asks for the state.

5 bytes

Byte Bit Field Type Meaning 0 Position unsigned 8-bit 0 fully open, 255 fully closed 1 Speed unsigned 8-bit 0 slowest, 255 fastest 2-3 Current signed 16-bit current limit of the move in mA, the grip force; not clamped by the firmware, keep it at or below the stepper's rated current (Force and speed) 4 7 Activate bit 1 activate the gripper, 0 deactivate 4 6 Action bit 1 go to the position, 0 idle 4 5 E-stop bit 1 raises the gripper E-stop error 4 4 Release direction bit read by the firmware but not used

The driver answers with Respond_Gripper_data_pack.

docs.title: Respond_Gripper_data_pack
docs.text:
ID 60driver → host4 bytes

The driver's answer to Send_gripper_data_pack: position, measured current, and the state bits. Python attributes gripper_position, gripper_current, gripper_activated, gripper_action_status, gripper_object_detection, gripper_temperature_error, gripper_timeout_error, gripper_estop_error, gripper_calibrated.

The frame (4 bytes)

Byte Bit Field Type Meaning 0 gripper_position unsigned 8-bit 0 fully open, 255 fully closed 1-2 gripper_current signed 16-bit measured current in mA 3 7 gripper_activated bit 1 activated 3 6 gripper_action_status bit 1 going to the position, 0 idle, auto-release or calibrating 3 5-4 gripper_object_detection 2 bits bit 5 is the low bit, bit 4 the high bit: 0 moving, 1 object detected while closing, 2 object detected while opening, 3 at the position 3 3 gripper_temperature_error bit 3 2 gripper_timeout_error bit 3 1 gripper_estop_error bit 3 0 gripper_calibrated bit 1 calibrated

The driver does not answer this command.

docs.title: UART commands
docs.text: The commands a gripper needs over the driver's serial port, for the firmware release this site describes. The kind, the argument type, the mode a command enters and what it prints are read from the firmware; the descriptions are written by hand. Over UART says where the port is and how it is used.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
#<Name> [number]
  • A Set/Get command sets the value when a number follows and prints the current value either way.
  • A Get command only prints.
  • An Action command does something; a number after it is ignored.
  • Names are case-sensitive, at most 19 characters; the number at most 19; the line ends with LF (CR before it is fine). 256000 baud, 8N1, 3.3 V.
  • A name the parser does not know is answered Unknown command.

docs.title: By group
docs.text:

docs.title: Gripper
docs.text: Command Kind Argument What it does Response #Gripper Set/Get int: 0 or 1 Whether this driver is a gripper. A gripper has it set and saved; #Default clears it, so set it again after restoring the defaults. the flag #Gripcal Action Starts the gripper calibration (the jaws find their end stops). Enters gripper calibration mode. Gripper calibration! #Gripinfo Get Prints the gripper state: calibrated, activated, end stops, position, current. the report #Gripstop Set/Get int: 0 or 1 The gripper E-stop bit. the bit #Gripact Set/Get int: 0 or 1 The activate bit. the bit #Gripcur Set/Get int: current in mA The current limit of gripper moves, the grip force. The firmware does not clamp it; keep it at or below the stepper's rated current (see Force and speed). the setpoint #Gripvel Set/Get int: 0 to 255 The speed setpoint of gripper moves. the setpoint #Grippos Set/Get int: 0 (open) to 255 (closed) The position setpoint; also activates the gripper, sets the action bit and goes to gripper mode. Enters gripper mode. the current position

docs.title: Driver setup
docs.text:
The driver commands a self-built gripper is configured with; Driver configuration is the procedure.

Command Kind Argument What it does Response #Kpiq Set/Get float: gain Kp of the Iq current loop; also sets Kpid. the current value #Kiiq Set/Get float: gain Ki of the Iq current loop; also sets Kiid. the current value #R Set/Get float: resistance in Ω The phase resistance of the motor (one coil). STEPFOC does not measure it; enter the datasheet value before Cal. the current value #L Set/Get float: inductance in H The phase inductance of the motor (one coil); enter the datasheet value before Cal. the current value #Kt Set/Get float: Nm/A The torque constant, found by calibration. the current value #Cal Action Runs the driver's motor calibration (see Driver configuration): enter PP, R and L first, with the pinion not yet in the rack. the calibration log #Save Action Writes the configuration to the EEPROM. Do it after calibration and after tuning. Save #Ilim Set/Get int: current in mA The driver's Iq current limit outside gripper mode; the firmware clamps it to 2800 mA. Gripper moves use Gripcur instead. the current limit #Tlim Set/Get int: temperature in °C The temperature at which the temperature error is raised; 75 by default. Temp limit N #Default Action Writes the factory defaults to the EEPROM, including the serial number, hardware version and batch date, and clears the gripper flag, heartbeat and watchdog. Back those up first. Loaded default config! #Term Set/Get int: 0 or 1 Enables the thermistor measurement and the temperature error (off by default). the setting #Cbw Set/Get float: bandwidth in Hz The current loop bandwidth calibration uses to compute Kpiq and Kiiq. the bandwidth #CANID Set/Get int: 0 to 13 The CAN node ID. Use 0 to 13: the firmware accepts 14 and 15, but the bootloader reserves them and a driver on one of those cannot be updated over CAN. Setting the ID also sets the bootloader's board ID. Kept over a power cycle after Save. the ID, or Invalid CAN ID #PP Set/Get int: pole pairs The motor's pole pairs: 50 for a 1.8° stepper, 75 for 1.2°, 100 for 0.9°, 125 for 0.72°. Calibration accepts only these values. the current value

docs.title: Status and utility
docs.text: Command Kind Argument What it does Response #Magnet Get Reads the encoder's magnet status. Magnet Good or Magnet Bad #Reset Action Resets the driver. From firmware 105 the reset lands in the bootloader, which waits 2 s for a flashing host and then starts the firmware again. nothing #Temp Get Prints the thermistor temperature. °C, or Temp Off while the thermistor is disabled #Mode Get Prints the control mode. Idle mode, Position control, Speed control, Current control, PD control, Open loop, Gripper mode #Vbus Get Prints the supply voltage. mV #Error Get Prints which errors are active. No errors! or In error state! followed by one line per active error #Clear Action Clears the errors and goes to idle. An error whose cause is still present comes straight back; a calibration error is cleared only by calibrating (or #Calibrated 1). Enters idle mode. Clear errors #Help Action Prints a short command reference. Added in firmware 108. the reference #Info Get Prints the driver's identity and state: hardware and firmware version, serial number, motor parameters, calibration, errors. the report #Calibrated Set/Get int: 0 or 1 The calibrated flag. #Calibrated 1 clears a calibration error without calibrating; the motor may still be uncalibrated. the flag #LED Set/Get int: 0 or 1 Turns the status LED on or off. the LED state

docs.title: Getting help
docs.text:
• Questions and discussion: the Source Robotics Discord.
  • A problem with the gripper's hardware or its files: an issue in the product repository; see Report a problem for what to include.
  • A problem with the firmware: an issue in the driver's repository; with the Python library, in Spectral-BLDC-Python; with the ROS 2 driver, in its repository.
  • A mistake on a page of this site: every page ends with a link to edit it and one to report it; see Contributing.
  • Orders and hardware: source-robotics.com.

Before you ask, Troubleshooting goes through the common symptoms, and the gripper's status tells most of what anyone will ask you for.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: This documentation lives in Source-Robotics/MSG-gripper-docs. A small fix can be made from the browser: the Edit it on GitHub link at the end of every page opens the page's source, and GitHub turns your change into a pull request. For anything larger, open an issue first.

docs.title: How the site is built
docs.text:
• The pages are Markdown, built with MkDocs and the Material theme; the repository's README.md says how to preview it locally.
  • The site describes one release of the STEPFOC firmware, named in versions.yml. The command IDs, frame lengths, the UART command list and what each prints in the API reference are read from the firmware's source at that release's tag by tools/sync_firmware.py; do not edit those facts in the pages. The descriptions of the commands are in docs/includes/can_commands.yml and uart_commands.yml, which list only the commands a gripper needs.
  • Every push runs a strict build (a broken link fails it) and the tool tests. A push to main publishes the site under its firmware version with mike.

docs.title: House rules
docs.text:
• Facts come from the firmware and the product repository. When a page and the firmware disagree, the firmware is right; fix the page, or report the firmware.
  • Spell commands exactly as the firmware does, even where the spelling looks wrong.
  • Write for someone who has the gripper in front of them and wants to do one thing: say what to do, in order, then why.
  • Three kinds of boxes: a note, a notice (damage) and a danger (injury). Use them for those, not for emphasis.
  • Images: under 2400 px on the long side, with a caption that says what the reader should see.

docs.title: Report a problem
docs.text:
Open an issue in the product repository for the gripper and its files, in the driver's repository for the firmware, or in Spectral-BLDC-Python for the Python library. Include:

  1. The gripper: bought or self-built, the rail and the stepper, the jaws.
  2. The firmware release the gripper runs: Send_Respond_Device_Info, or #Info over UART, which also carries the driver's configuration and errors.
  3. The gripper's status when the problem happens: the state and error bits of Respond_Gripper_data_pack, or #Gripinfo.
  4. What you did and what happened: the commands, in order, with their position, speed and current, and the answers.
  5. How it is connected: the robot or the adapter, the cable, the termination; a photo helps more than a description.

For a problem with this documentation, the Report it link at the end of the page opens an issue in the documentation repository with the page already named.
